title: Session-mix jitter portrait — latency & cost notes
content:
Purpose
---
Quick exploratory notes mapping how session composition (conversation length distribution + cold-start rate + token variance) drives observed jitter at p50/p90/p99 and the downstream per-10k-token cost. This is intentionally informal: sketches, ASCII micro-charts, and a set of actionable flags for follow-up measurement. No polished graphs here — we want an operational portrait to inform next round of focused benches.

Background and motivation
---
Several customers report intermittent latency spikes that don't correlate with instance-level metrics (GPU utilization looks fine) but do align with changes in session mix (more short chats / more calls with many system messages). Hypothesis: the combination of small worst-case token bursts + cache miss patterns amplifies observed jitter due to scheduling and batching windows. We want to quantify the effect across realistic mixes and estimate the unit-cost impact if we tighten SLOs (i.e., move from p95 to p99 guarantees).

Bench config (summary)
---
- Hardware: 1x A100-40GB (core), 4x A10G for edge variants.
- Runtime: branch bench-jitter-2027 (kernel selection tweaks enabled).
- Models: llama-3-medium-8k-like (float16 path), and a quantized variant q4_0-equivalent for cost comparisons.
- Network: simulated intra-region 1ms baseline, 12ms introduced jitter scenario for edge.
- Cache config: KV cache hit rates swept at {0%, 25%, 50%, 75%}.
- Session mixes tested (each mix = 10k sessions over 30 minutes):
  * Mix A (short-heavy): 70% conversations <= 40 tokens, 25% 40-200, 5% >200. Cold-start 45%.
  * Mix B (balanced): 40% <=40, 40% 40-200, 20% >200. Cold-start 25%.
  * Mix C (long-heavy): 15% <=40, 35% 40-200, 50% >200. Cold-start 10%.

Key metric definitions
---
- p50/p90/p99 latency (server-side, token generation tail excluded).
- Jitter index = p99 / p50 ratio (higher => more extreme tails relative to median).
- Cost-per-10k-tokens = assigned GPU minutes * cloud-cost-per-minute normalized to token count (rough estimate w/ model throughput baseline).

Representative results (text tables and sparklines)
---
Note: values are approximate from the exploratory runs; use for relative comparisons only. Quantized runs have lower cost but higher median latency in some cold-start-heavy mixes.

Table: p50 / p90 / p99 (ms) for core float model, KV hit=50%
Mix A (short-heavy): p50=38ms | p90=92ms | p99=270ms  (Jitter idx=7.1)
Mix B (balanced):    p50=85ms | p90=160ms | p99=340ms  (Jitter idx=4.0)
Mix C (long-heavy):   p50=220ms| p90=420ms | p99=620ms  (Jitter idx=2.8)

ASCII sparkline (p99 over mixes as KV hit sweeps 0%->75%)
KV 0%:  Mix A [#######........] 270ms  Mix B [##########.....] 340ms  Mix C [############..] 620ms
KV 25%: Mix A [#####..........] 210ms  Mix B [#########......] 300ms  Mix C [###########...] 560ms
KV 50%: Mix A [###............] 170ms  Mix B [######.........] 260ms  Mix C [#########......] 480ms
KV 75%: Mix A [#..............] 120ms  Mix B [#######........] 200ms  Mix C [#######........] 380ms

Cost sketch (per-10k-tokens equivalent)
- Float core model (A100 baseline): Mix A ~ $1.10 / 10k tokens; Mix B ~ $0.95 / 10k; Mix C ~ $1.05 / 10k (long sessions amortize overheads but increase compute).
- Quantized variant (q4-like): Mix A ~ $0.42 / 10k; Mix B ~ $0.36 / 10k; Mix C ~ $0.48 / 10k.
- Observed cost delta when tightening p99 SLO (i.e., adding warm prewarmed slots to absorb spikes): +12–28% cost depending on mix (highest for Mix A).

Interpreting the portrait
---
1) Short-heavy mixes are the worst for jitter. Why? Small sessions interact poorly with batching windows and increase the fraction of cold-KV requests per unit time. A high cold-start rate multiplies the tail.
2) Long-heavy mixes have higher median latency (more tokens to generate) but lower jitter index; tail events are less extreme relative to median because per-session overheads get amortized.
3) KV cache hit rate is a strong lever — moving from 0% to 75% hit rate reduces p99 by ~40–45% in short-heavy scenarios. Operational implication: invest in hot-prefix caching and TTL tuning for short-turn workloads.
4) Quantization reduces cost substantially but can raise median latency in cold-start/unbatched scenarios; this is visible in Mix A where q4 warms slower in our runtime due to per-kernel overhead.
5) Tightening p99 SLOs by reserving slots (prewarm) mainly helps Mix A but has diminishing returns for Mix C and drives notable cost increases.

Operational action flags (next steps)
---
- Flag 1: Implement a microbench that reproduces Mix A with controlled cold-start bursts in staging and collect kernel-level timers (JIRA-OPS-9982). Need per-request trace IDs to map scheduling decisions to latency spikes. Owner: Arjun. Target: 2027-03-22.
- Flag 2: Add KV-prefetch experiment for short sessions (preload most-likely prefixes for top 10% of user prompts). Quick A/B in canary. Owner: Leah. Target: 2027-04-01.
- Flag 3: Evaluate quantized warmup optimizations (reduce per-kernel setup cost). PR in runtime: link above. Owner: Carlos. Target: 2027-03-29.
- Flag 4: SLO policy experiment: dynamic prewarm only when short-session ratio > 50% (avoid linear cost increase). Implement as rollout rule in console. Product stub: PRO-ROLL-224. Owner: Maya. Target: 2027-04-12.

Open questions and measurement gaps
---
- We haven't isolated network-level jitter vs runtime scheduling. Need packet-level traces for edge region results.
- The cost model here is simplified (normalized minutes). Need to re-run with actual committed Dedicated pricing and autoscale behaviors to get customer-facing numbers.
- Mixing multi-tenant noise: all benches were single-tenant. Multi-tenant GPU virtualization may amplify p99; follow-up required.

Quick troubleshooting checklist for support
---
If a customer reports intermittent spikes with short chats:
- Check short-session fraction in last 1h (>50% => matches Mix A).
- Check KV cache hit rate and recent model variant change.
- Look for increase in cold-start ratio (new user surge, post-deploy restarts).
- Try enabling dynamic prewarm rule (if available); if not, escalate to eng-observability for canary of KV prefetch experiment.

Notes to self (loose thoughts)
---
- Consider adding a tiny stateful prefix cache colocated with fronting process to handle the "first token" work for short chats. Might be cheaper than prewarming full slots.
- Potential follow-up talk for infra summit: "Jitter by session archetype — why short chats are sneaky expensive" — 20m slot.
